subject: social-science
question: What is a stereotype?
options: A kind of government office
A festival celebrated in many states
A fixed idea about a whole group of people that ignores what individuals are really like
A rule written down in the Constitution
hint: A stereotype puts every person in a group into one box, whatever they are actually like.

subject: social-science
question: What does it mean to be prejudiced against someone?
options: To judge them badly before knowing anything about them
To be curious about where they come from
To agree with everything they say
To meet them for the first time
hint: The word means to pre-judge — to decide before you know.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is an example of a stereotype?
options: Saying that India has many languages
Saying that people from a particular state are all good at business
Saying that your friend Rahul is good at maths
Saying that Kerala has a long coastline
hint: A statement about one person, or a plain fact, is not a stereotype. A claim about everyone in a group is.

subject: social-science
question: How are a stereotype and discrimination different?
options: A stereotype is against the law but discrimination is not
Discrimination happens only in schools
A stereotype is a fixed idea in the mind; discrimination is acting on it and treating someone unfairly
They mean exactly the same thing
hint: One is a thought, the other is something done to a person.

subject: social-science
question: A new student joins and everyone assumes she must be shy because she is from a small town. What is this?
options: Discrimination, because she has been punished
A stereotype, because they decided what she is like before knowing her
A fact, because small towns are quieter
Good manners, because they are being careful with her
hint: Nobody has treated her unfairly yet — but they have already decided what she is like.

subject: social-science
question: Why are stereotypes unfair even when they sound positive?
options: They still stop a person being seen as an individual, and they put pressure on those who do not fit
They are only unfair if they are said out loud
They are unfair only to adults
They are never unfair if they are meant kindly
hint: Think of a child told she must be good at studies because of where her family comes from.

subject: social-science
question: Ravi refuses to sit next to a classmate because of a rumour he heard about her family. What has Ravi allowed to guide him?
options: Evidence, because a rumour is a kind of proof
Nothing at all — where you sit does not matter
The school rules
Prejudice, because he judged her without knowing anything himself
hint: He acted on something he heard rather than anything he knows.

subject: social-science
question: Which is the best way to weaken a stereotype about a group?
options: Getting to know people from that group as individuals
Waiting for the government to pass a law
Repeating the stereotype until it sounds silly
Avoiding people from that group
hint: A stereotype survives on distance. It rarely survives an actual friendship.

subject: social-science
question: Where do children usually pick up stereotypes from?
options: Only from the internet
From what they hear around them — family, friends, films and jokes
Children are born with them
Only from textbooks
hint: Nobody is born with a stereotype. It has to be learned from somewhere.

subject: social-science
question: Which statement is a fact rather than a stereotype?
options: People who speak that language are always loud
People of that community are all wealthy
Children from that city never study hard
India has more than twenty official languages
hint: A fact can be checked. A stereotype is a claim about everybody in a group.

subject: social-science
question: Why is it wrong to say 'all people from that community are the same'?
options: Because the sentence is grammatically incorrect
Because groups do not really exist
Because it is impolite to talk about communities at all
Because every group contains millions of different people who think and live differently
hint: Ask whether everyone in your own class is the same as you.

subject: social-science
question: A teacher always asks the boys to carry the sports equipment and the girls to decorate. What is she acting on?
options: The wishes of the students
A school rule about safety
A stereotype about what boys and girls are suited to
A law of the country
hint: Nobody asked the students what they were good at or wanted to do.

subject: social-science
question: What is the danger of believing a stereotype about yourself?
options: You will become very confident
You will forget your own name
You may stop trying at things you have been told your group is not good at
Nothing at all happens
hint: A child told girls are bad at maths may stop putting her hand up.

subject: social-science
question: Two people from the same village behave very differently. What does this show?
options: That one of them must be pretending
That the village has two separate parts
That where a person comes from does not decide who they are
That stereotypes are usually correct
hint: If the stereotype were true, both would behave the same way.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these shows prejudice turning into discrimination?
options: A shopkeeper thinks a customer looks unfriendly
A shopkeeper closes early on a festival day
A shopkeeper refuses to serve a customer because of the community he belongs to
A shopkeeper charges everyone the same price
hint: Discrimination is the moment the thought becomes an action against someone.

subject: social-science
question: Why do people sometimes hold on to stereotypes even after meeting someone who does not fit?
options: Because stereotypes are protected by law
Because stereotypes are always true
Because they cannot remember the meeting
They treat that person as an exception instead of changing their idea
hint: You may have heard someone say, 'Yes, but he is different from the rest.'

subject: social-science
question: What is the difference between noticing that people are different and being prejudiced?
options: Noticing difference is against the law
Prejudice only counts if it is written down
There is no difference between them
Noticing difference is simply seeing; prejudice adds the idea that one kind of person is worse
hint: Diversity is a fact. Prejudice is a judgement laid on top of it.

subject: social-science
question: A film shows every character from one region as a fool. What is the film doing?
options: Breaking a law of physics
Reporting the news accurately
Helping that region become better known
Spreading a stereotype to a very large audience
hint: Films reach millions, so the fixed idea they show travels a long way.

subject: social-science
question: Why is it useful to ask 'How do I know that?' when you hear a claim about a group?
options: It makes you check whether you have any real reason to believe it
It proves the claim is correct
It is required by the Constitution
It is a polite way of ending a conversation
hint: Most stereotypes fall apart the moment somebody asks for the evidence.

subject: social-science
question: What is the best short description of prejudice?
options: A written government order
A feeling of curiosity about others
An opinion formed about someone before knowing them, usually an unfair one
A careful judgement made after long study
hint: The 'pre' in the word is doing the work.

subject: social-science
question: What does discrimination mean?
options: Treating someone worse than others because of the group they belong to
Choosing the best player for a team after a fair trial
Noticing that people look different from one another
Giving everybody the same thing
hint: The unfairness comes from the group, not from anything the person has done.

subject: social-science
question: A hostel refuses a room to a student because of his religion. This is discrimination based on:
options: Handwriting
Height
Examination marks
Religion
hint: Look at the reason given for the refusal.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is NOT discrimination?
options: A club that refuses entry to people of one community
An employer who pays women less for the same work
A school that admits only children of one caste
A running race where the fastest runner wins
hint: In a fair race, everyone competes under the same rules.

subject: social-science
question: What is 'untouchability'?
options: A kind of medical treatment
The cruel practice of treating some people as impure and keeping them apart from others
A game played in villages
A rule about washing hands before meals
hint: It was a caste practice, and the Constitution abolished it.

subject: social-science
question: Being teased for being short, dark or overweight is discrimination based on:
options: Language
Income
Physical appearance
Religion
hint: The teasing is about how the person looks.

subject: social-science
question: Why is discrimination based on appearance harmful even when it is called 'just a joke'?
options: It is harmful only if a teacher hears it
It is not harmful at all
Jokes are against the law in India
The person is still made to feel worth less for something they cannot change
hint: Ask who is laughing and who is being laughed at.

subject: social-science
question: A family is refused a house on rent because of the community they belong to. What is this?
options: An example of diversity
A rule made by the municipality
Discrimination, because the reason has nothing to do with them as tenants
A fair business decision by the owner
hint: Nothing about their ability to pay rent or care for the house was in question.

subject: social-science
question: What is inequality?
options: A kind of election
A situation where everybody is treated the same
A situation where some people have far less opportunity or respect than others
A mathematics chapter about greater than and less than
hint: Think about who gets a chance and who does not.

subject: social-science
question: Why do people who face discrimination often also end up poorer?
options: Because they choose not to work
Because money is distributed by lottery
There is no connection between the two
Being shut out of schools, jobs and housing over generations leaves families with less
hint: One closed door leads to the next: no school, then no job, then no savings.

subject: social-science
question: Two children do the same work. One is paid less because she is a girl. This is discrimination based on:
options: Gender
The type of work
The number of hours
Age
hint: The work was the same. Only one thing was different.

subject: social-science
question: A shop puts up a board saying people of a certain community will not be served. In India this is:
options: Required by law in some states
Allowed, because a shop is private property
Allowed if the shopkeeper explains his reason
Illegal, because the Constitution forbids such discrimination
hint: Article 15 forbids discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these best shows discrimination in school?
options: Dividing the class into two teams for a quiz
Making some children sit separately and eat apart from the rest
Giving a prize to the student who read the most books
Asking students to line up by their roll number
hint: Look for the rule that separates children by who they are rather than what they did.

subject: social-science
question: Why is discrimination different from an ordinary disagreement between two people?
options: It can only happen between strangers
It always involves shouting
It targets a person for belonging to a group, and often follows them everywhere they go
It is settled by an apology
hint: A quarrel ends. Discrimination waits at the next door too.

subject: social-science
question: What can a student do when they see a classmate being excluded because of their background?
options: Laugh, since it is not their own problem
Include them, and tell a teacher if it continues
Wait quietly for it to stop by itself
Join in so as not to seem different
hint: Doing nothing leaves the child alone with it.

subject: social-science
question: Someone is refused a job even though he scored highest in the test, because of his caste. Why is this wrong as well as illegal?
options: Because he should have applied elsewhere
Because tests should not be used for jobs
The decision ignored the only thing that should have mattered — how well he could do the job
Because the employer did not explain the decision
hint: He had already proved he was the best candidate.

subject: social-science
question: 'Diversity' and 'discrimination' are not the same thing. Which statement is correct?
options: They are two words for the same idea
Diversity means people differ; discrimination means some are treated worse for those differences
Discrimination happens only where there is no diversity
Diversity always causes discrimination
hint: Difference by itself harms nobody. What is done about it can.

subject: social-science
question: A village well may be used by everyone except one group of families. This is an example of:
options: A rule of the panchayat about cleanliness
A water shortage
Discrimination based on caste
An accident
hint: Water was available. Only certain families were kept from it.

subject: social-science
question: Why does discrimination often continue for many years even after a law bans it?
options: Because courts are not allowed to act
Because laws stop working after some years
Because nobody has heard about the law
Laws can change what people may do, but attitudes take longer to change
hint: A rule can be written in a day. A habit of mind takes longer.

subject: social-science
question: What is the first thing that makes discrimination possible?
options: The belief that some people are worth less than others
A shortage of money
A large population
The existence of many languages
hint: Before anyone is shut out, somebody has decided they matter less.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is an example of positive action to reduce inequality?
options: Reserving seats in colleges for groups kept out of education for generations
Closing schools in villages
Charging higher fees to poorer students
Refusing admission to students from one community
hint: The aim is to open a door that has been shut for a very long time.

subject: social-science
question: What is the Constitution of India?
options: A list of India's states and their capitals
A book of Indian history
The country's supreme rulebook, setting out how it is governed and what rights people have
A collection of speeches by leaders
hint: Every other law in the country must agree with it.

subject: social-science
question: When did the Constitution of India come into force?
options: 26 November 1949
2 October 1950
26 January 1950
15 August 1947
hint: That is why 26 January is celebrated as Republic Day.

subject: social-science
question: Which article of the Constitution abolishes untouchability?
options: Article 51A
Article 17
Article 21
Article 370
hint: It abolishes the practice and makes it punishable.

subject: social-science
question: Article 15 forbids discrimination on which grounds?
options: Marks scored in examinations
Religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
Height, weight and eyesight
The language a person prefers to read
hint: Learn the five grounds — they cover most of what people are born into.

subject: social-science
question: What does 'equality before the law' mean?
options: Only judges are equal
Everyone must study the same subjects
Everyone earns the same amount of money
The same law applies to everyone, whoever they are
hint: It is about how the law treats you, not about wealth.

subject: social-science
question: The Preamble to the Constitution promises justice, liberty, equality and:
options: Loyalty
Prosperity
Victory
Fraternity
hint: It means a spirit of brotherhood among all the people of India.

subject: social-science
question: Why did the makers of the Constitution include Fundamental Rights?
options: So that the Constitution would be longer
To replace the need for courts
So that every citizen would have protections the government itself cannot take away
Because other countries asked India to
hint: A right that the government could remove at will would not protect anyone.

subject: social-science
question: What can a citizen do if a Fundamental Right is violated?
options: Nothing — the rights are only suggestions
Go to the High Court or the Supreme Court
Wait for the next election
Write to a newspaper, which is the only remedy
hint: A right you cannot enforce is not much of a right.

subject: social-science
question: How does the Constitution treat India's diversity?
options: It ignores the question entirely
It protects it, allowing people to follow their own religion, language and culture
It allows only some states to be diverse
It asks everyone to adopt one language and one religion
hint: Look at the freedom of religion and the protection of languages.

subject: social-science
question: What is the Right to Equality meant to correct?
options: Differences in people's heights
Centuries of some people being treated as lesser because of birth
The uneven distribution of rainfall
The shortage of schools in cities
hint: The Constitution was written in a country where birth had long decided a person's place.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is a Fundamental Duty of every Indian citizen?
options: To learn three languages
To join the armed forces
To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood among all people
To vote for a particular party
hint: The Fundamental Duties sit alongside the rights, asking something of the citizen in return.

subject: social-science
question: Why is it important that the Constitution applies to the government too?
options: Because a government that is above the law could take away people's rights at will
It does not apply to the government
Because ministers are elected
Because the government writes the newspapers
hint: The point of a supreme rulebook is that nobody stands above it.

subject: social-science
question: The Constitution allows special provisions for some groups. Why is this not a contradiction of equality?
options: Treating everyone identically would leave groups held back for generations exactly where they are
Because equality applies only to adults
Because the provisions are temporary jokes
Because the Constitution often contradicts itself
hint: Two runners do not start level if one begins several laps behind.

subject: social-science
question: Which body wrote the Constitution of India?
options: The Supreme Court
The United Nations
The Constituent Assembly
The British Parliament
hint: Its members were drawn from all over India and debated for nearly three years.

subject: social-science
question: How long did the Constituent Assembly take to complete the Constitution?
options: Just under three years
Nearly twenty years
One year exactly
About three weeks
hint: It sat from December 1946 and adopted the Constitution in November 1949.

subject: social-science
question: What does the Right to Freedom of Religion guarantee?
options: That only the largest religion is protected
That religion may not be discussed
That everyone must attend a place of worship
That a person may follow, practise and spread the religion of their choice, or none
hint: The choice belongs to the person, not to the state or the neighbours.

subject: social-science
question: A state government passes a law that allows discrimination by caste. What happens to it?
options: The courts can strike it down for violating the Constitution
It applies only to that state and cannot be questioned
It becomes valid because a government passed it
It replaces the Constitution in that state
hint: No law may sit above the supreme rulebook.

subject: social-science
question: Why is the Constitution described as a 'living document'?
options: It expires after fifty years
It can be amended as society changes, while its basic principles remain
It is read aloud every year
It is printed on special paper
hint: It has been amended more than a hundred times without losing its foundations.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these best explains why the Constitution begins with 'We, the people of India'?
options: It is a greeting to visitors
It shows the Constitution's authority comes from the people themselves
It names the members of the Assembly
It is a translation of an older law
hint: Ask who is speaking in those first four words.

subject: social-science
question: What is the Right against Exploitation meant to stop?
options: Students being given homework
Practices such as forced labour and the employment of young children in hazardous work
Long journeys to school
Shops charging high prices
hint: It protects people who could otherwise be made to work against their will.

subject: social-science
question: In April 2014, what did the Supreme Court of India rule in the NALSA case?
options: That transgender persons must be recognised as a third gender with full constitutional rights
That no change in the law was needed
That the matter was for each state to decide separately
That transgender persons must choose to be male or female
hint: The judgment was delivered on 15 April 2014.

subject: social-science
question: What does it mean that a person may decide their own gender identity, as the Court held?
options: The decision is made by a majority vote in the family
Gender identity cannot be changed on any document
The person themselves decides, rather than a doctor or an official deciding for them
The government assigns a gender at the age of eighteen
hint: The Court called this the right to self-identification.

subject: social-science
question: Which fundamental rights did the Supreme Court say applied to transgender persons?
options: Only rights connected with property
Only the right to vote
The rights to equality, against discrimination, to expression and to life with dignity
No fundamental rights, but some legal benefits
hint: The Court read Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 as covering them.

subject: social-science
question: Why did the Supreme Court's recognition of a third gender matter in everyday life?
options: It allowed transgender persons to obtain documents such as passports and voter cards in their own identity
It made school uniforms optional
It had no practical effect at all
It changed the design of the national flag
hint: Without matching documents, ordinary tasks like opening a bank account become impossible.

subject: social-science
question: What is the older Indian word often used for a transgender community, which the judgment discussed?
options: Sarpanch
Zamindar
Hijra
Diwan
hint: The Court noted such communities have a long history in India.

subject: social-science
question: The Court also directed that transgender persons be treated as which category for education and jobs?
options: Applicants who must always be placed first
A separate country within India
A group not needing any special measures
Socially and educationally backward classes, so they could receive reservations
hint: The aim was to open opportunities long closed to them.

subject: social-science
question: Why had many transgender persons found it hard to get schooling or work before this ruling?
options: They faced discrimination and often had no documents recording who they were
Because they were not interested in studying
Because schools did not exist in their areas
Because the law required them to work at home
hint: Two things were missing: fair treatment, and papers that matched their identity.

subject: social-science
question: What is the correct way to speak about a transgender classmate?
options: Use the name and pronouns they ask you to use
Use whichever name you find easier
Avoid speaking to them at all
Ask the whole class to vote on it
hint: It costs nothing to call somebody what they ask to be called.

subject: social-science
question: Which statement about the 2014 judgment is correct?
options: It was a law passed by a state assembly
It was an order from a district court in Delhi
It was an announcement by a private organisation
It was decided by the Supreme Court, the highest court in India
hint: NALSA stands for the National Legal Services Authority, which brought the case.

subject: social-science
question: Why is it wrong to stare at or mock a person who is transgender?
options: It is not wrong, only impolite
It is wrong only if a policeman is watching
It is wrong only in schools
It denies them the dignity that the Constitution guarantees every person
hint: Article 21 protects the right to live with dignity.

subject: social-science
question: What does 'discrimination on the ground of sex' in Article 15 include, according to the Court?
options: Only discrimination at work
Discrimination because of a person's gender identity
Only discrimination between men and women
Nothing beyond marriage laws
hint: The Court read the word broadly, so the protection reached further.

subject: social-science
question: Before 2014, what problem did transgender persons face with official forms?
options: Most forms offered only 'male' or 'female', leaving them unable to record who they were
There were no official forms in India
Forms were only printed in English
Forms had to be filled in by a lawyer
hint: A form with only two boxes forces a false answer on some people.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these best describes the purpose of the NALSA judgment?
options: To change the school syllabus
To decide a property dispute
To create a new state
To bring a group long treated as outsiders inside the protection of the Constitution
hint: Ask who was left out before, and who was included after.

subject: social-science
question: A transgender student is refused admission to a school. What does the 2014 judgment mean for this?
options: The school may decide as it wishes
The refusal is discrimination and is against the Constitution
The student must apply to a special school
The judgment applies only to adults
hint: Recognition of rights is not limited by age.

subject: social-science
question: What does the word 'dignity' mean in the phrase 'right to live with dignity'?
options: Being famous
Being treated as a person worthy of respect
Holding a government post
Owning expensive things
hint: Dignity is not something you buy or earn — it belongs to everyone.

subject: social-science
question: Why did the Court say self-identification should not require a medical operation?
options: Because operations are illegal in India
Because a person's identity is about who they are, not about a surgical procedure
Because operations are expensive
Because doctors refused to help
hint: Making surgery a condition would put the decision back into someone else's hands.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these actions would help a transgender person most in a school?
options: Excusing them from all activities
Giving them a separate classroom
Making sure they are included in classes, teams and friendships like anyone else
Asking them to explain themselves to the school
hint: Inclusion, not separate arrangements, is what the judgment points towards.

subject: social-science
question: The NALSA judgment is an example of which body protecting rights?
options: The judiciary — the courts
The executive — the council of ministers
The legislature — Parliament
The Election Commission
hint: It was a court decision, not a law passed by Parliament.

subject: social-science
question: Why do court judgments matter even when Parliament has not passed a law?
options: Because judges are elected by the people
They do not matter until a law is passed
Courts can interpret the Constitution, and their reading binds the whole country
Because judgments last only one year
hint: The Constitution is the higher rulebook, and the courts say what it means.

subject: social-science
question: What is the simplest thing a classmate can do to support a transgender friend?
options: Report them to the school office
Treat them as an ordinary friend and stand up for them when others do not
Ask them personal questions in front of others
Tell them they should keep it a secret
hint: The most useful support is usually the least dramatic.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: What position did Dr B. R. Ambedkar hold while the Constitution was being written?
options: President of India
Chief Justice of India
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Chairman of the Drafting Committee
hint: The Drafting Committee prepared the text the Assembly debated.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: What was Dr Ambedkar's role in the first government of independent India?
options: He held no position in government
He was the first Law Minister
He was the first President
He was the first Prime Minister
hint: He held the law portfolio in Nehru's first cabinet.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: As a schoolboy, what did Dr Ambedkar experience because of his caste?
options: He was made head boy of the school
He was made to sit apart from other children and was not allowed to drink from the common water pot
He was given extra lessons by his teachers
He was excused from examinations
hint: His own school days are one of the clearest accounts of untouchability we have.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Which article of the Constitution, which Dr Ambedkar helped shape, abolished untouchability?
options: Article 17
Article 12
Article 356
Article 44
hint: It abolishes the practice in any form and makes it an offence.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Why is Dr Ambedkar often called the chief architect of the Indian Constitution?
options: He paid for the printing of the Constitution
He designed the building where it was written
He was the oldest member of the Assembly
He led the committee that drafted it and defended its provisions through long debates
hint: An architect draws the plan and argues for it — that is what he did.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Dr Ambedkar studied abroad at which universities?
options: He never attended a university
At universities in Japan and China
Columbia University in America and the London School of Economics
Only at universities inside India
hint: He was among the most highly educated Indians of his time.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Why did Dr Ambedkar place so much importance on education?
options: He believed education was the strongest tool people had to escape an unjust system
He wanted to become a teacher
He thought only educated people should vote
He believed education mattered less than wealth
hint: His own life was the argument: education was how he was heard.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: What did Dr Ambedkar mean by saying political equality is not enough without social equality?
options: That voting should be stopped
That society matters more than the Constitution
A person may have a vote and still be treated as an outcaste in daily life
That equality is impossible
hint: One vote every five years does not change how neighbours behave every day.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: In 1956, Dr Ambedkar and many of his followers converted to which religion?
options: Zoroastrianism
Buddhism
Jainism
Sikhism
hint: He saw it as a path out of a social order built on caste.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Which honour was conferred on Dr Ambedkar in 1990, long after his death?
options: The Padma Shri
The Bharat Ratna
The Nobel Peace Prize
The Param Vir Chakra
hint: It is India's highest civilian award, and it was given posthumously.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: What did Dr Ambedkar argue was the root of caste discrimination?
options: The number of languages in India
A shortage of land in villages
A social order that fixed a person's worth by the family they were born into
The climate of the Indian subcontinent
hint: His objection was to birth deciding a person's place for life.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Dr Ambedkar campaigned for the right of all people to use public wells and temples. Why did this matter so much?
options: Because temples were the largest buildings in villages
Because wells were the only source of drinking water in India
Being kept from shared spaces marked people publicly as lesser, every single day
Because he wanted the wells to be rebuilt
hint: The exclusion was visible to the whole village, which was part of its cruelty.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Where was Dr Ambedkar born, and in which year?
options: In Pune, in 1869
In Mhow, in 1891
In Kolkata, in 1885
In Delhi, in 1901
hint: His birth anniversary on 14 April is marked across India.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Which of these best describes Dr Ambedkar's approach to changing society?
options: Using law, argument and education rather than violence
Withdrawing from public life
Asking for help from foreign governments
Leading an armed rebellion
hint: His weapons were a pen, a book and a constitutional article.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Why did Dr Ambedkar support reservations in education and government jobs?
options: To open doors to communities kept out of both for centuries
To reduce the number of applicants
To make government offices smaller
Because he thought examinations were unfair to everyone
hint: Where a group has been shut out for generations, an open door is not enough on its own.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Dr Ambedkar famously described the Constitution's rights as needing something more to be real. What?
options: A larger army
A society willing to live by them
More printing presses
Support from other countries
hint: He warned that a good constitution can fail in the hands of an unwilling people.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: What does the phrase 'Educate, Agitate, Organise', associated with Dr Ambedkar, urge people to do?
options: Learn, speak up against injustice, and work together
Study quietly and avoid public life
Leave the country to find work
Wait for leaders to solve their problems
hint: Three verbs, in a deliberate order: know it, name it, then act together.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: Why is 14 April observed across India?
options: It is Dr Ambedkar's birth anniversary
It marks the end of British rule
It is the anniversary of the NALSA judgment
It is the day the Constitution came into force
hint: Do not confuse it with 26 January.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: What did Dr Ambedkar mean when he said the Constitution could be as good or as bad as those who work it?
options: Even the best rules depend on the honesty of the people who apply them
That the Constitution should be rewritten often
That constitutions do not matter
That only lawyers can understand it
hint: The document does not enforce itself.

subject: social-science
topicLabel: Dr Ambedkar & the Fight Against Caste
question: How is Dr Ambedkar's work connected to a child's school life today?
options: He designed the school timetable
He has no connection with schools
The right to be admitted, seated and treated equally in school rests on principles he fought for
He wrote the mathematics textbook
hint: Think of the boy who was not allowed to touch the water pot, and what changed.

subject: social-science
question: Who led the Nazi Party and became the ruler of Germany in the 1930s?
options: Winston Churchill
Otto von Bismarck
Karl Marx
Adolf Hitler
hint: He became Chancellor of Germany in January 1933.

subject: social-science
question: What did the Nazis wrongly claim about Germans of Jewish faith?
options: That they should lead the government
That they had recently arrived from another continent
That they were the best scientists in Germany
That they were responsible for Germany's problems — a false and cruel accusation
hint: Blaming a whole group for a country's troubles is prejudice on a national scale.

subject: social-science
question: What were the Nuremberg Laws of 1935?
options: Rules for a football tournament
Laws that took away the citizenship and rights of German Jews
Laws that gave equal rights to all Germans
Laws protecting German forests
hint: Prejudice was written into the law book itself.

subject: social-science
question: Jews in Nazi Germany were forced to wear a yellow star. What was the purpose of this?
options: To help them find each other in a crowd
To show which school they attended
To mark them out in public so they could be identified and treated differently
To honour them for their service
hint: A visible mark makes discrimination easy for everyone to carry out.

subject: social-science
question: What is the Holocaust?
options: A treaty signed at the end of the war
A battle fought in North Africa
A famine in eastern Europe
The murder of about six million Jews by the Nazis during the Second World War
hint: Millions of others, including Roma people and disabled people, were also killed.

subject: social-science
question: Anne Frank is remembered for what?
options: Inventing a code used in the war
The diary she kept as a Jewish girl hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam
Leading an army against Germany
Writing the Nuremberg Laws
hint: She was a teenager, and her diary is read all over the world.

subject: social-science
question: How did the Nazis prepare ordinary people to accept the mistreatment of Jews?
options: Through years of propaganda in newspapers, films, posters and school lessons
By asking each family to decide for itself
They made no attempt to persuade anyone
By holding a national vote on the question
hint: The cruelty came last. Persuasion came first.

subject: social-science
question: Why is it important to study the Holocaust in school?
options: To learn the names of German cities
Because it is an interesting adventure story
To decide which country was strongest
So that we recognise where prejudice can lead if it is not stopped early
hint: The lesson is about the road, not only the destination.

subject: social-science
question: During which war did the Holocaust take place?
options: The Second World War
The Crimean War
The First World War
The Cold War
hint: The war ran from 1939 to 1945.

subject: social-science
question: What does the word 'propaganda' mean?
options: A type of government building
A careful scientific study
A law passed by a parliament
Information spread to make people believe something, often one-sided or untrue
hint: Its purpose is to persuade, not to inform.

subject: social-science
question: Jewish children in Nazi Germany were expelled from ordinary schools. What did this do to them?
options: It improved their education
It had no effect on their lives
It gave them more time to play
It cut them off from friends and learning, and marked them out as different
hint: Think of what school gives a child besides lessons.

subject: social-science
question: What lesson does the Nazi period teach about laws?
options: Every law passed by a government is fair
Laws can never be questioned
Only old laws can be unjust
A law is not automatically just — laws themselves can be deeply wrong
hint: The Nuremberg Laws were properly passed, and they were monstrous.

subject: social-science
question: Some people in Europe hid Jewish neighbours at great risk to themselves. What does this show?
options: That hiding people was easy and safe
That individuals can choose to act rightly even when their government does not
That everyone in Europe agreed with the Nazis
That the Nazis did not really object
hint: They are remembered because their choice was rare and dangerous.

subject: social-science
question: What was a concentration camp?
options: A camp where the Nazis imprisoned people they had singled out, under terrible conditions
A holiday camp for German schoolchildren
A place where treaties were signed
A camp where German soldiers trained
hint: People were sent there for who they were, not for anything they had done.

subject: social-science
question: Which idea did the Nazis use to justify treating some people as less than human?
options: The false belief that their own group was a superior race
The belief that education matters most
The belief that all people are equal
The belief that Germany should have no army
hint: Every large-scale cruelty begins with the claim that some people count for less.

subject: social-science
question: Why did many Jewish families try to leave Germany in the 1930s?
options: Because German winters were cold
Because they wanted to see other countries
Because the Nazis paid them to leave
Because they had lost their rights and were no longer safe there
hint: By 1935 they were no longer citizens of their own country.

subject: social-science
question: What is the connection between the Nazi story and the study of prejudice?
options: There is no connection between them
It shows that prejudice exists only in Europe
It shows how a stereotype can grow into discrimination, then into law, then into violence
It shows that stereotypes are usually harmless
hint: Trace the steps in order — each one made the next easier.

subject: social-science
question: After the war, leading Nazis were put on trial at Nuremberg. Why did this matter?
options: It decided which country would rebuild Germany
It was only a ceremony with no verdicts
It established that people can be held responsible for crimes even when their government ordered them
It chose the new German flag
hint: 'I was following orders' was rejected as a defence.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is the safest thing to do when you hear a joke that mocks a whole community?
options: Repeat it to others to see what they think
Laugh so that nobody feels awkward
Say that you do not find it funny, and explain why
Say nothing and remember it
hint: Silence is usually read as agreement.

subject: social-science
question: What does the phrase 'never again', often said about the Holocaust, mean?
options: A promise never to visit Germany
A decision to forget what happened
A rule that history must not be taught
A promise to recognise and stop such persecution before it can happen again
hint: It is a promise about the future, which is why the past is taught.

subject: social-science
question: What was racial segregation in the United States?
options: A tax paid by all citizens
A method of counting the population
A system that kept black and white people apart in schools, buses and public places
A style of American music
hint: Separate schools, separate seats, separate drinking fountains.

subject: social-science
question: Who was Rosa Parks?
options: A judge who ended segregation
The first black president of the United States
A black woman who refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in 1955
A singer who wrote protest songs
hint: Her refusal in Montgomery, Alabama, sparked a long bus boycott.

subject: social-science
question: What is a boycott?
options: A vote taken in secret
A kind of court order
Refusing to use or buy something as a way of protesting
A tax on imported goods
hint: In Montgomery, black residents simply stopped riding the buses.

subject: social-science
question: Who delivered the famous 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963?
options: Martin Luther King Jr
Barack Obama
Nelson Mandela
Abraham Lincoln
hint: He spoke in Washington to a crowd of more than two hundred thousand.

subject: social-science
question: What method did Martin Luther King Jr urge his followers to use?
options: Armed rebellion
Non-violent protest
Leaving the country
Refusing to speak to anyone
hint: He was influenced by Mahatma Gandhi's methods in India.

subject: social-science
question: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 do?
options: It ended the Second World War
It outlawed discrimination based on race, colour, religion, sex or national origin
It made education compulsory worldwide
It created the United Nations
hint: It was the law that finally made segregation illegal.

subject: social-science
question: Ruby Bridges became famous in 1960 for what?
options: Winning an Olympic medal
Being the first black child to attend an all-white school in her city, escorted by officers
Becoming a judge at a young age
Writing a book about segregation
hint: She was six years old, and crowds shouted at her on the way in.

subject: social-science
question: Why did segregation continue for many years even after slavery was abolished?
options: Because nobody had noticed the problem
Laws and customs kept black people separate and unequal long after they were free
Because black people preferred to live separately
Because slavery was never actually abolished
hint: Freedom from slavery was not the same as equality.

subject: social-science
question: How is the American struggle against segregation similar to the fight against untouchability in India?
options: Both involved a group kept out of shared spaces and treated as lesser by birth
Both were caused by a shortage of schools
They have nothing in common
Both were about taxes on farmers
hint: Different countries and histories, but the same shape of injustice.

subject: social-science
question: Dr King and Dr Ambedkar both used which tool against injustice?
options: Armies and weapons
Support from foreign rulers
Withdrawal from public life
Law, argument and organised peaceful protest
hint: Both were highly educated men who chose persuasion and the law.

subject: social-science
question: What were the 'Jim Crow' laws?
options: Laws about immigration from Europe
Rules for American football
Laws protecting farmers' crops
State laws in the American South that enforced segregation
hint: They kept segregation in place for decades after slavery ended.

subject: social-science
question: Segregated schools for black children were usually worse funded. Why did that matter for the future?
options: Poorer schooling limited the jobs and opportunities open to children later in life
It made those schools more popular
It did not matter, since all schools teach the same
It affected only the school buildings
hint: Unequal schooling turns into unequal lives.

subject: social-science
question: What does 'civil rights' mean?
options: The right to own a car
The rules of polite behaviour
Rights that belong only to soldiers
The rights every citizen has to be treated equally and take part in public life
hint: Civil here means belonging to citizens.

subject: social-science
question: The Montgomery bus boycott lasted for over a year. What does its length tell us?
options: That changing an unjust system takes sustained effort and sacrifice
That the boycott failed
That the protest was not serious
That the buses were not needed
hint: Many walked miles to work every day for more than a year.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is the clearest example of segregation?
options: A stadium with numbered seats
A bus with seats for the elderly
Separate drinking fountains marked for black and white people
A school with separate classrooms for each grade
hint: Look for the division made by who a person is, not by age or ticket.

subject: social-science
question: Why is Rosa Parks' refusal remembered as an act of courage?
options: The bus was empty at the time
She was certain nothing would happen to her
She knew she could be arrested, and was, but refused to accept an unjust rule
The driver had asked her to stay seated
hint: Courage is not the absence of risk.

subject: social-science
question: What did the Supreme Court decide in the Brown v. Board of Education case of 1954?
options: That segregation should continue for ten more years
That only universities must be integrated
That separate schools for black and white children were unconstitutional
That schools should charge fees
hint: 'Separate but equal' was rejected as a contradiction.

subject: social-science
question: What is the main lesson of the American civil rights movement for students today?
options: That only presidents can change a country
That protest never achieves anything
That injustice ends by itself with time
Ordinary people acting together can change laws that seem permanent
hint: A seamstress, a preacher and a six-year-old girl all appear in this story.

subject: social-science
question: Barack Obama became president of the United States in 2009. Why was this seen as historic?
options: He was the first president from a small state
He was the first black president of a country that had once enforced segregation by law
He was the youngest president ever elected
He was the first president to visit India
hint: Measure the distance from 1955 in Montgomery to 2009 in Washington.

subject: social-science
question: Why do many countries teach the history of segregation even though it happened elsewhere?
options: Because it is required by the United Nations
Because it has no connection to their own country
Because the pattern of one group being treated as lesser appears in every society
Because it is the easiest history to teach
hint: The particular story is American. The pattern is not.

subject: social-science
question: What is a gender stereotype?
options: A fixed idea about what boys or girls should be like or should do
A subject taught in school
A rule written in the Constitution
A medical test done at birth
hint: It decides in advance what someone can do, based only on being a boy or a girl.

subject: social-science
question: Why is telling a boy 'boys don't cry' harmful?
options: It teaches him to hide his feelings instead of dealing with them
It helps him make friends more easily
It is not harmful, only old-fashioned
It makes him physically stronger
hint: Feelings do not disappear because a child is told not to show them.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is a gender stereotype?
options: Saying that a chef needs training
Saying that some people enjoy cooking
Saying that cooking is women's work
Saying that food is needed by everyone
hint: Look for the sentence that assigns a task to one gender.

subject: social-science
question: A girl is discouraged from playing football because 'it is a boys' game'. What is happening?
options: She is being protected from injury
She is being denied an opportunity because of a gender stereotype
She is being treated equally
She is being given good sporting advice
hint: Nobody asked whether she was good at it or enjoyed it.

subject: social-science
question: Why do gender stereotypes limit boys as well as girls?
options: They affect only girls, never boys
They give boys too many choices
They push boys away from things like caring, cooking or dancing that they may want to do
They make boys work harder at school
hint: A box has walls on every side.

subject: social-science
question: In many homes, girls are expected to do housework while brothers are not. What is this an example of?
options: A sign that girls enjoy housework more
A rule made by the government
An unequal division of work based on gender
A fair sharing of duties
hint: Ask whether the same expectation is placed on both children.

subject: social-science
question: What is the effect on a girl's studies when she carries most of the housework?
options: It gives her extra time for homework
She has less time and energy to study, however capable she is
It improves her marks
It has no effect at all
hint: Time spent one way cannot be spent another.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is NOT decided by whether someone is a boy or a girl?
options: What subjects they can be good at
Nothing — gender decides everything
Their favourite colour, which is fixed at birth
The games they are capable of enjoying
hint: Ability in a subject has nothing to do with gender.

subject: social-science
question: Toy shops often place dolls in one aisle and building sets in another. What does this teach children?
options: Which toys are most expensive
Nothing at all
That some toys, and the skills they build, belong to one gender only
How to find toys quickly
hint: A child learns what is 'for them' long before anyone says it aloud.

subject: social-science
question: A father takes leave from work to look after a new baby. What does this show?
options: That caring for children is a parent's job, not only a mother's
That he does not enjoy his work
That the mother is unwell
That he has broken a rule
hint: Ask why the same choice by a mother would surprise nobody.

subject: social-science
question: How does a stereotype about girls and mathematics affect real results?
options: Girls who hear it may lose confidence and stop trying, which then seems to prove the stereotype
It makes girls better at mathematics
It has no effect on anything
It changes the answers to mathematics problems
hint: This is why a false belief can appear to come true.

subject: social-science
question: Which statement about housework is accurate?
options: It should be done only by children
It is naturally suited to women
It is not really work
It is work, whoever does it, and it can be shared by everyone in a family
hint: Notice that it is usually unpaid and often unnoticed.

subject: social-science
question: A boy wants to learn classical dance and is teased. What is the best response from his classmates?
options: Tell him to keep it secret
Join in the teasing so he changes his mind
Ask a teacher to stop the dance classes
Support him, because interests are not decided by gender
hint: Some of India's finest classical dancers are men.

subject: social-science
question: What does it mean to say gender roles are 'learned'?
options: That they cannot ever change
That only adults have them
Children pick them up from family, school and society rather than being born with them
That they are taught as a school subject
hint: If they are learned, they can also be unlearned.

subject: social-science
question: Which is the strongest reason for sharing housework equally at home?
options: Because children enjoy chores
Because it makes the house cleaner
Because the government requires it
Everyone benefits from the home, so everyone should contribute to running it
hint: The argument is about fairness, not about tidiness.

subject: social-science
question: A school offers woodwork only to boys and needlework only to girls. What should it do instead?
options: Cancel both subjects
Offer both to all students and let them choose
Keep the arrangement, since it is traditional
Offer them only in alternate years
hint: The fair test is whether the choice belongs to the student.

subject: social-science
question: Why is 'she throws like a girl' an insult that carries a stereotype?
options: It is a compliment about accuracy
It uses being a girl as a way of saying someone is bad at something
It describes a real physical rule
It is a technical term used in sport
hint: Ask what the phrase assumes before it is even finished.

subject: social-science
question: How do films and advertisements often strengthen gender stereotypes?
options: By avoiding pictures of people
By repeatedly showing men in one kind of role and women in another
By showing every kind of person equally
They have no influence on what people believe
hint: Repetition is what makes an idea start to feel normal.

subject: social-science
question: What is the difference between a biological fact and a gender stereotype?
options: There is no difference
A biological fact is about the body; a stereotype is a social expectation added on top
A biological fact can be changed by opinion
A stereotype is always true
hint: Only one of the two can be argued away.

subject: social-science
question: What is the best way for a class to challenge gender stereotypes?
options: Separate boys and girls for all activities
Share tasks and opportunities equally and question assumptions when they come up
Let only teachers decide everything
Never discuss the subject
hint: The change is made in ordinary daily arrangements.

subject: social-science
question: Indra Nooyi is known for leading which global company?
options: Microsoft
PepsiCo
Tata Steel
Infosys
hint: She was its chief executive from 2006 to 2018.

subject: social-science
question: In which Indian city was Indra Nooyi born and educated?
options: Lucknow
Chennai
Jaipur
Bhopal
hint: She studied in Chennai and Kolkata before going to the United States.

subject: social-science
question: Saina Nehwal made history in which sport?
options: Hockey
Badminton
Athletics
Tennis
hint: She reached world number one in 2015.

subject: social-science
question: What did Saina Nehwal achieve at the London Olympics in 2012?
options: She carried the Indian flag at the closing ceremony
She won a gold medal in tennis
She won a bronze medal, the first Olympic medal for India in badminton
She won India's first Olympic medal of any kind
hint: Her medal opened the door for Indian badminton.

subject: social-science
question: Dipa Karmakar is remembered as the first Indian woman to do what?
options: Captain the Indian cricket team
Compete in gymnastics at the Olympic Games
Referee an international match
Win a gold medal in swimming
hint: She qualified for the Rio Olympics in 2016.

subject: social-science
question: How close did Dipa Karmakar come to a medal at the Rio Olympics in 2016?
options: She withdrew before the event
She won the gold medal
She finished fourth in the vault, missing bronze very narrowly
She did not reach the final
hint: Fourth at the Olympics is the hardest place to finish.

subject: social-science
question: Kalpana Chawla was the first woman of Indian origin to do what?
options: Travel into space
Win a Nobel Prize
Climb Mount Everest
Fly a fighter aircraft
hint: She first flew aboard the space shuttle in 1997.

subject: social-science
question: Kalpana Chawla trained as which kind of engineer?
options: A chemical engineer
A civil engineer
A mining engineer
An aerospace engineer
hint: She studied in Punjab and then in the United States.

subject: social-science
question: What happened during Kalpana Chawla's second space mission in 2003?
options: She returned safely and retired
The mission was cancelled before launch
The shuttle landed in the wrong country
The shuttle Columbia broke apart on its return and the whole crew was lost
hint: She is remembered for how she lived, not only for how she died.

subject: social-science
question: What do the lives of these four women have in common?
options: They all played the same sport
They were all born in the same city
They all worked for the government
Each succeeded in a field where few Indian women had gone before
hint: Business, badminton, gymnastics and space — four different doors.

subject: social-science
question: Why does it matter that girls hear about women like Saina Nehwal and Kalpana Chawla?
options: Seeing someone like yourself succeed makes an ambition feel possible
It does not matter who the examples are
Because their stories are required in examinations
Because girls cannot learn from men's stories
hint: It is hard to aim at something you have never seen anyone do.

subject: social-science
question: Dipa Karmakar performed the Produnova, one of gymnastics' most difficult vaults. What does this show?
options: That she was willing to attempt the hardest routine to compete with the best
That gymnastics has no difficult moves
That she avoided risk in competition
That the vault was easy for everyone
hint: Very few gymnasts in the world have attempted it.

subject: social-science
question: Indra Nooyi has spoken about the difficulty of balancing work and family. Why is this worth knowing?
options: It shows that women often face demands at home that their male colleagues do not
It proves women should not lead companies
It shows she did not enjoy her job
It has nothing to do with equality
hint: The extra load is part of what makes the climb steeper.

subject: social-science
question: What did Saina Nehwal's success change for young Indian players?
options: It ended all other sports in India
It made badminton an Olympic sport
It showed that an Indian could reach the very top in world badminton
It changed the rules of the game
hint: Players who followed her have spoken about watching her win.

subject: social-science
question: Which statement about these four women is accurate?
options: They each inherited their position from family
They all worked in the same country
They were all given their positions without competing
They reached the top of fields long dominated by men
hint: Each of them competed against the best in the world.

subject: social-science
question: What does the phrase 'breaking the glass ceiling' mean?
options: Reaching a senior position that women were previously kept out of, though nobody admitted the barrier existed
Winning a sporting trophy made of glass
Leaving a job to start a business
Repairing the roof of a building
hint: The barrier is invisible, which is exactly the point of the phrase.

subject: social-science
question: Kalpana Chawla grew up in Karnal, a small town in Haryana, and became an astronaut. What does her path show?
options: That her family already worked in space research
That where a person begins need not decide how far they go
That only people from large cities can become astronauts
That she left India as a young child
hint: Very few girls from small Indian towns in the 1960s could have imagined that career.

subject: social-science
question: How should a school best encourage girls to aim high?
options: Ask them to choose safer careers
Praise them only for good behaviour
Give them the same opportunities, coaching and expectations as boys
Set easier goals for them
hint: Lower expectations are a kindness that costs a great deal.

subject: social-science
question: A girl says she wants to be an engineer and is told to try teaching instead. What is happening?
options: Her ambition is being narrowed by a stereotype about suitable work for women
She is being given expert career advice
She is being treated exactly as a boy would be
She is being told a fact about engineering
hint: Ask whether a boy saying the same thing would get the same reply.

subject: social-science
question: What is the most useful lesson from these four life stories?
options: That only exceptional people should try
That women succeed only in sport
That success depends mainly on luck
That ability is not decided by gender, and opportunity is what most often decides who succeeds
hint: Ask what each of them needed besides talent.

subject: social-science
question: What is the sex ratio of a population?
options: The number of children in each family
The total number of people in a country
The number of females for every thousand males
The proportion of people who can read
hint: It is a simple count that reveals a great deal.

subject: social-science
question: In several Indian states the sex ratio has been much lower than expected. What does that indicate?
options: That more boys are born naturally in those states
That girls move away after birth
That the counting was done wrongly
That girls have been valued less, and in some places prevented from being born
hint: Nature produces roughly equal numbers, so a large gap has a human cause.

subject: social-science
question: What does the PCPNDT Act of 1994 prohibit?
options: All medical tests during pregnancy
Using medical tests to find out the sex of an unborn child
Women working as doctors
The building of new hospitals
hint: The tests themselves are useful for health; using them to select a child's sex is banned.

subject: social-science
question: Why is it illegal in India to tell parents the sex of an unborn child?
options: Because doctors cannot determine it accurately
Because that knowledge has been used to prevent girls from being born
Because the test is very expensive
Because parents are not interested
hint: The law targets the use of the information, not the medicine.

subject: social-science
question: What is the 'Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao' scheme about?
options: Building roads in villages
Providing electricity to farms
Training young men for jobs
Saving and educating the girl child
hint: The name translates directly: save the daughter, teach the daughter.

subject: social-science
question: In which year was the Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao scheme launched?
hint: It was launched at Panipat in Haryana in January 2015.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these reasons has been given for preferring sons, and why is it mistaken?
options: That sons support parents in old age — yet daughters do so just as often
That sons are required by law to inherit
That sons are born healthier, which is medically proven
That daughters cannot attend school
hint: The belief was never a fact, and daughters have disproved it for generations.

subject: social-science
question: How does the practice of dowry contribute to families treating a daughter as a burden?
options: It makes a daughter's marriage costly, so some families see her as an expense
It makes daughters wealthier than sons
It has no effect on how families think
It is required by the Constitution
hint: Dowry itself is illegal in India, but the custom persists in places.

subject: social-science
question: Under Indian law, what right does a daughter have in her family's ancestral property?
options: Half of what a son receives
A right only if there is no son
No right at all
The same right as a son
hint: The Hindu Succession Act was amended in 2005 to make daughters equal coparceners.

subject: social-science
question: What happens to a society where far fewer girls are born than boys?
options: The imbalance creates serious social problems for the whole community, not only for women
The population becomes wealthier
Schools become easier to run
Nothing changes
hint: A generation missing millions of women affects everyone in it.

subject: social-science
question: Which of these is the strongest argument for educating girls?
options: Every child has an equal right to learn, and an educated girl gains choices for life
It is cheaper than educating boys
It keeps girls occupied until marriage
Educated girls demand smaller dowries
hint: The right comes first; the benefits follow from it.

subject: social-science
question: A family sends its son to a private school and its daughter to a cheaper one. What is this?
options: Discrimination, because the child's schooling is decided by gender rather than need or ability
A sensible way to save money
Equal treatment of both children
A rule set by the government
hint: Ask what would happen if their genders were swapped.

subject: social-science
question: Why do many girls drop out of school earlier than boys?
options: They are often kept back for housework, care of siblings, or early marriage
Because schools refuse to admit them
Because they are not interested in learning
Because they find studying more difficult
hint: The reasons are usually about what is expected of them at home.

subject: social-science
question: What does 'gender equality' mean?
options: That men and women must do identical jobs
That the number of boys and girls in every class must match
That differences between people are ignored
That people have the same rights, opportunities and respect whatever their gender
hint: It is about equal standing, not identical lives.

subject: social-science
question: Which article of the Constitution allows the state to make special provisions for women and children?
options: Article 15
Article 51
Article 19
Article 32
hint: The same article that forbids discrimination also permits measures to correct it.

subject: social-science
question: Why is a law banning sex determination difficult to enforce?
options: Because the test is impossible to perform
The test can be done quietly, and both the doctor and the family may keep it secret
Because courts refuse to hear such cases
Because the law is not written down
hint: Where nobody involved will complain, the offence is hard to detect.

subject: social-science
question: What can schools do to help change attitudes towards girls?
options: Avoid discussing the subject with students
Hold separate classes for girls in every subject
Give girls equal opportunities in class, sport and leadership, and teach why it matters
Ask girls to take fewer examinations
hint: Children carry what they see at school back into their homes.

subject: social-science
question: Kerala has among the highest female literacy rates in India. What does this suggest?
options: That when girls are educated and valued, whole regions do better on health and development
That literacy has no connection with development
That Kerala has fewer girls than other states
That literacy is measured differently there
hint: Compare Kerala's health figures with the national average.

subject: social-science
question: What is the first step an ordinary family can take towards valuing a daughter equally?
options: Keeping her at home for safety
Arranging her marriage early
Waiting for the government to act
Giving her the same food, schooling and freedom to choose as a son
hint: Equality begins with the ordinary decisions made every day.

subject: social-science
question: Why is the phrase 'a daughter is not a burden' at the heart of this topic?
options: Because treating a daughter as a cost is the belief that leads to every unfairness she faces
Because it applies only to poor families
Because it is a slogan used in advertisements
Because it refers to carrying heavy loads
hint: Change the belief and the practices that follow it lose their reason.
